annotations.title: The God of Pharao.
annotations.text: [1] The name of God, which eſſentially is proper only to the three Diuine Perſons of the B. Trinitie, and incommunicable to anie creature (Sap. 14.) is neuertheles by ſimilitude attributed in holie Scripture to other perſons. As (Exod. 22. v. 8.) Iudges, or princes, are called goddes, [2]for the eminent authoritie and powre which they haue from God. So Moyſes was conſtituted the Iudge and God of Pharao, [3]not only to punish him, for his obſtinacie, and finally to compel him to diſmiſſe the Iſraelites out of Ægypt, but alſo to terrifie him ſo in the meane time, that he being otherwiſe a mightie King, and extremly and often afflicted by Moyſes, yet durſt neuer lay violent handes vpon him, leſt himſefe, and al his nation ſhould preſently haue bene deſtroyed. As S. Hilarie (lib. 7. de Trinitate) & S. Gregorie (ho. 8. in Ezech.) note vpon this place. Likewiſe Prieſts are called goddes [4] (Exod 22. v. 28.) for their ſacred function, pertaining to Religion and Seruice of God. Prophetes alſo are called Videntes, Seers [5] (1. Reg. 9.) becauſe by participation of diuine knowledge, they ſee ſometimes the ſecretes of other mens hartes, things ſupernatural, and future contingent, though properly and naturally onlie God almightie is Scrutator cordis, the ſearcher of the hart, and knoweth al things (Sap. 1.) Againe S. Peter ſaieth (2. Epiſt. c. 1.) that iuſt men are made partakers of diuine nature. VVhich is rather more rhen to participate in name. Al which titles rightly perteined to Moyſes, being in life Holie, in knowledge a Prophete, in function a [6] [7] Prieſt, and in powre a Prince. In the ſame ſenſe of participation, Saintes are called our Mediators, Aduocates, Redemers, Deliuerers, and the like.

annotations.title: I vvil indurate.
annotations.text: According to our purpoſe mentioned in the Annotations vpon the 9. chap. to the Romans, we shal here recite the ſumme of S. Auguſtine's doctrine (Ser. 88. de tempore) touching the hard queſtion: How God did indurate Pharao's heart. And withal we shal briefly explicate, according to the doctrine of the ſame, & other moſt learned Fathers of the Church, the true ſenſe of this and like places, by which Zuinglius, Caluin, Beza, and other Sectaries [1], would proue that God not only permitteth, but alſo commandeth, inclineth, enforceth, and compelleth men to do that which is ſinne: yea that God is the author, internal mouer, & enforcer, that man tranſgreſſeth; though they denie that God ſinneth, or is cauſe of the malice of ſinne. For example, Zuinglius [2] (Ser. de prouidentia Dei, ca. 5) ſaith: Numen ipſum auctor eſt eius, quod nobis eſt iniuſtitia, illi vero nullatenus eſt. The diuine power itſelf is author of that thing, which to vs is iniuſtice, but to him in nowiſe is. And a little after, Cum igitur Angelum tranſgreſſorem facit, & hominem, ipſe tamen tranſgreſſor non conſtituitur. When therefore God maketh Angel, and man tranſgreſſor, yet himſelf is not made a tranſgreſſor. Cha. 6. Vnum igitur atque idem facinus, puta adulterium aut homicidium, quantum Dei eſt auctoris, motoris, impulſoris, opus eſt, crimen non eſt: quantum hominis eſt, crimen ac ſcelus eſt. Therefore the ſelfſame act, as adulterie or manſlaughter, as it is of God the author, mouer, enforcer, is a worke, is not a crime: but as it is of man, is a crime, & a wicked act. [3] Caluin (li. 8. Inſtit. c. 17. para. 11.) affirmeth that the devil, & the whole band of the wicked cannot conceiue, nor endeavour, nor do anie miſchief, niſi quantum Deus permiserit, imo niſi quantum ille mandarit. But ſo farre as God permitteth (which all Catholics firmly believe) nay but ſo far as he commandeth: which all Catholics abhorre and deteſt. Likewiſe (li. 2. c. 4. para. 4.) alleging God's words, ſaying he had aggrauated, and hardened Pharao's heart, affirmeth, that which God did more, beſides not mollifying his heart, was, quod obſtinatione pectus eius obfirmandum Satanæ mandauit, that he committed his heart to Satan to be obdurated with obſtinacie: making God the author, and Satan only the miniſter of hardening Pharao's heart. [4] Beza folowing this race (in Reſpon. ad Caſtallionem, Aphoriſmo 22.) ſaith, God ſo vvorketh by evil inſtruments, that he doth not only ſuffer them to worke, nor only moderateth the euent, ſed etiam vt excitet, impellat, moueat, regat, atque adeo (quod omnium eſt maximum) etiam creet, vt per illa agat quod conſtituit: but alſo ſtirreth them up, driueth them forward, moueth them, ruleth them, and (which is moſt of all) euen createth them, that by them he may vvorke that which he appointed. All which (ſaith he) God doth rightly, and vvithout anie iniuſtice. So indeed theſe men ſay, when they are preſſed with the blaſphemous abſurditie, that they make God author and cauſe of ſinne, which neceſſarily and euidently foloweth of their doctrin. [5] For by the very light of nature it is clear, that the commander or enforcer is author of that euil which an other doth by his commandment or enforcement, and by all law of nature and nations, divine and human, is condemned as culpable and guiltie of the fault, which the other committeth: but theſe Miniſters ſay (in the places aboue cited) God commandeth, enforceth and vvorketh all that a ſinner doth: Ergo, God by this doctrin muſt be author, culpable, and guiltie of ſinne. Which is ſo blaſphemous, and horrible to Chriſtian ears, that they dare not ſay it in expreſs terms. Seing then God is ſaid to haue indurated Pharao's heart, and all confeſſe that induration of heart is a moſt grievous ſinne, the controuerſie is: [6] VVhether God commanded, enforced, and wrought the induration in Pharao's heart, or only permitted it? Or what els God did to Pharao, whereby his heart was indurate; and finally by whom it was properly indurate, by God, or by Pharao himſelf? All which S. Auguſtine explicateth [7], laying firſt this ground (which euerie one is faithfully and firmly to believe) that God neuer forſaketh any man, before he be firſt forſaken by the ſame man [8]: yea God alſo long expecteth, that a ſinner which much and often offendeth, conuert and liue [9]. But when the ſinner abideth long in his wickednes, of the multitude of ſins riſeth deſperation, of deſperation is engendered obduration. For when the impious is come to the depth of ſins, he contemneth [10]. Obduration therefore cometh not of God's power compelling, but is engendered by God's remiſnes or indulgence, and ſo not diuine power, but diuine patience did harden Pharao's heart. How often ſoeuer therefore our Lord ſaith: I wil indurate the heart of Pharao, he would nothing els to be vnderſtood, but I will ſuſpend my plagues and punishments, whereby I will permit him through mine indulgence to be obdurate againſt me [11]. Perhaps ſome will aske, why did God by ſparing him let him be indurate? Why did God take from him his wholeſome punishment? I anſwer ſecurely: this was done, becauſe Pharao, for the huge heape of his ſins [12], deſerued not as a child to be corrected vnto amendment, but as an enemie was ſuffered to be indurate. For of them, whom God's mercie ſuffereth not to be indurate, it is written: [13] God ſcourgeth euerie child whom he receiueth. And in an other place: [14] Whom I loue I correct and chaſtiſe. Againe: [15] Whom God loueth he chaſtiſeth. Let no man therefore with Pagans and Manichees preſume to reprehend or blame God's iuſtice, but certainly believe, that not God's violence made Pharao indurate, but his owne wickednes, and his vntamed pride againſt God's precepts. Againe, what els is it to ſay, I vvil indurate his heart, but when my grace is abſent from him, his owne wickednes will obdurate him? [16] To know this by examples: water is congealed with vehement cold; but the heat of the ſunne coming vpon it, is reſolued, and the ſunne departing, it freezeth againe. [17] In like maner by the lazineſs of ſinners, charitie waxeth cold, & they are hardened as ice: but when the heat of God's mercie commeth vpon them, they are againe ſoftened. So Pharao without pittie or compaſſion afflicting the Hebrews, became as hard as ice, but God's hand touching him with afflictions, he made humble ſupplication, that Moyſes and Aaron would pray to God for him, promiſing what they demanded: againe, when the plagues were remoued, he was more indurate againſt God and his people, then before. Whereby we ſee, God's gentlenes, indulgence, and ſparing of Pharao, not his rigour, not his will or ſet purpoſe, but his permiſſion, and Pharao's owne wilful malice hardened his heart, and brought him to obſtinate contempt of God's commandments. And therefore God did only indurate him, in that common phraſe of ſpeaking, [18] as a father, or a maſter hauing brought up his child or ſeruant delicately, and not ſufficiently punished his frequent faults, whereby he becometh worſe and worſe, deſperate and obdurate, at laſt the father or maſter ſaith: I haue made thee thus bad as thou art, I by ſparing thee and ſuffering thee to haue thine owne pleaſure, haue nouriſhed thy perverſeneſs, and careleſnes: yet he ſaith not this, as though by his will and intention, but by his goodnes and gentlenes the man became ſo wicked. it may here be demanded againe; why did not our Lord ſo mercifully punish Pharao, as wholy to reclaim him, for it ſemeth that had benne greateſt mercie; [19] and God dealeth ſo with ſome, why doth he not with all, that all might be ſaued? Firſt it is moſt iuſtly and rightly aſcribed to their iniquitie, which deſerue to be indurate: againe why this ſinner is reclaimed, and not an other of the ſame ill deſerts, is to be referred to God's inſcrutable iudgements, which are often ſecrete, neuer vniuſt. [20] Let it therefore ſuffice piouſly and humbly to believe, that as Moyſes teſtifieth, [21] God is faithful and without anie iniquitie, juſt and right: and as the royal Prophet alſo profeſſeth, [22] Thou art not a God that vvilt iniquitie, and as the Apostle teacheth, [23] there is no iniquitie with God. By all which and ſome more to the ſame effect (which we omit) S. Auguſtine concludeth againe, that properly Pharao hardened his owne heart [24], God only by beſtowing benefits vpon him, which he abuſed, and not plaguing him ſo much, as he deſerued, but letting him liue, and reigne, and perſecute the Church for the time, vntil he and all his armie were in the midſt of the ſea. [25] Whither (as the ſame learned father noteth (ſer. 89.) their owne deſperate boldnes drew them, vaine furie through their owne madnes prouoking them to go ſo farre, where God not working, but only ceaſing to continue his miracle, the waters returning to their owne nature, and meeting together inuolued and drowned them all. [26] Other like expoſitions the ſame learned father hath in other places. As, q. 18. ſuper Exodum, he teacheth that Pharao being already ſo wicked through his owne fault, other things were done to him and his people, which partly were to the correction of others, and might haue bene to his, but he abuſing all, became worſe & worſe, by God's ſuffering and diſpenſation, not only for his juſt, but euidently juſt punishment. Li. 5. cont. Iulian c. 3. touching the ground of tentation he alleageth the Apoſtle ſaying: [27] Euerie one is tempted of his ovvne concupiſcence, abſtracted and allured: but touching one kind of God's puniſhing ſome, that are ouerwhelmed in obſtinate ſins [28], he alleageth the ſaying of another Apoſtle: [29] God hath deliuered them into paſſions of ignominie, and into a reprobate ſenſe, to do thoſe things that are not conuenient, for God deliuereth them (ſaith he) conueniently: that the ſame ſins are made both punishments of ſins paſt, and are deſerts of puniſhments to come. Yet he maketh not the wills euil, but vſeth the euil as he will, who cannot will anie thing vniuſtly. Againe, q. 24. It appeareth (ſaith he) that the cauſes of induration of Pharao's heart, were not only for that his Enchanters did like things (to thoſe which Moyſes and Aaron did) but the very patience of God [30], by which he ſpared him. God's patience according to men's hearts is profitable to ſome to repentance, to ſome vnprofitable to reſiſt God, & perſiſt in euil; yet not of it-ſelfe vnprofitable, but through the euil heart. Briefly. q. 36. I have hardened Pharao's heart, that is, I haue bene patient ouer him and his ſeruants. Epiſt. 105. God doth not indurate by imparting malice, but by not imparting mercie (or grace.) Li. de Proedeſt. & Grat. c. 4. God is ſaid to indurate him, [31] whom he will not mollifie. So, to make him blinde whom he will not illuminate. So alſo to repel him, whom he will not call. And c. 6. what is that to ſay: I wil indurate his heart [32], but I will not mollifie it? cap. 14. it ought to have auailed Pharao to ſaluation, that God's patience deferring his juſt and deſerued punishment, multiplied vpon him frequent ſtripes of miracles, or miraculous punishments. Cap 15. [33] Did not Nabuchodonoſor repent being puniſhed after innumerable impieties, and recouered the kingdome which he had loſt? But Pharao by puniſhment became more obdurate, and periſhed. Both were men, both kings, both perſecutors of God's people. both gently admonished by punishments. VVhat then made their ends diuers, but that the one feeling God's hand mourned in remembrance of his owne iniquitie, the other by his freewill fought againſt God's moſt merciful veritie? Neither is this the doctrin of S. Auguſtine alone, [34] but of other Doctors alſo. [35] Origen (li. 3. Periarch. c. de. Libert. arbitrij) ſaith, the Scripture ſheweth manifeſtly, that Pharao was indurate by his owne will. For ſo God ſaid to him: Thou vvouldeſt not: If thou wilt not diſmiſſe Iſrael. [36] [37] S. Baſil. (Orat. quod Deus non ſit auctor malorum) ſaith, God beginning with leſſe ſcourges, proceeded with greater and greater to plague Pharao, but did not mollifie him being obſtinate, neither yet did punish him with death, vntil he drowned himſelfe, when he preſumed through pride, to paſſe the ſame way, by which the juſt went, ſuppoſing the redde ſea would be paſſable to him, as it was to the people of God. [38] S. Chryſoſtom (ho. 67. in Ioan) God is ſaid in holie Scripture to haue indurate ſome, and deliuered ſome into reprobate ſenſe, not for that theſe things are done by God (coming indeed to man's owne proper malice) but becauſe God iuſtly leauing men, theſe things happen to them. And (in cap. 1. Rom.) He deliuered (into reprobate ſenſe) in nothing els, but he permitted. [39] S. Damaſcen (li. 4. ca. 20. de fide orthodoxa). It is the maner of holie Scripture to call the permiſſion of God his act. As, He hath given them the ſpirite of compunction; eyes, that they may not ſee: and ears that they may not heare [40], and the like; all which are to be vnderſtood not as proceding of God's action, but as of God's permiſſion, to wit, for man's free power of working. [41] S. Hierom. (Epiſt. 150. reſp. ad q. 10.) Not God's patience is to be accuſed, but their hardneſs who abuſe God's goodnes to their owne perdition. [42] Theodoret. (q. 17. in Exod.) It is to be noted, that if Pharao had bene euil by nature, he had neuer changed his minde. And (after diuers mutations recited, how ſometimes he would diſmiſſe Iſrael, other times he would not) all theſe (ſaith he) Moyſes recorded to teach vs, that neither Pharao was of peruerſe nature, neither did our Lord God make his mind hard and rebellious. For he that now inclineth to this part, now to that, plainly sheweth freewill of the mind. [43] S. Gregorie (li. 11. ca. 8. Moral.) God is ſaid to indurate by his iuſtice, when he doth not mollifie a reprobate heart. And (li. 31. c. 11.) Our Lord is ſaid to haue indurated Pharao's heart, not that he brought the hardneſs itſelf, but for that his deſerts ſo requiring, he did not mollifie it, with ſenſibilitie of feare infuſed from aboue. [44] S. Iſidorus (li. 2. ca. 19. de ſummo bono.) Sinne is permitted for puniſhment of ſinne, when a ſinner, for his deſert forſaken of God, goeth into an other worſe ſinne. Finally conference of holie Scriptures, as in other hard places, ſo in this, giveth light for better vnderſtanding thereof. For diuers places do not only ſhew that in all theſe reſiſtances, mutations of mind, and obſtinacie of heart, Pharao was neuer depriued of freewill, as the Doctors before cited do note, [45] but alſo expresſly attribute the act of induration to himſelf. Cha. 8. v. 15. Pharao ſeeing that reſt was given, he hardened his ovvne heart. V. 32. where the Latin readeth in the paſſiue voice, ingrauatum eſt cor Pharaonis, Pharao's heart was hardened, which is more obſcure, the Hebrew ſaith actiuely, & the proteſtants ſo tranſlate [46], Pharao hardened his hart this time alſo. Likewiſe cha. 9. v. 7. the Hebrew ſayeth, Pharao's heart hardened itſelf. Alſo v. 35. He hardened his ovvne heart, he and his ſeruants. Cha. 13. v. 15. When Pharao had indurated himſelfe. And, 1. Reg 6. v. 6. Why do you harden your hearts, as Ægypt and Pharao hardened their heart? All which are reconciled with the other texts, that ſay God indurated Pharao's heart, vnderſtanding that phraſe in like ſenſe to this. (cha. 15. v. 4.) [47] God hath caſt Pharao his chariots, and his armie into the ſea. Where God only permitted, and no way forced Pharao and his armie, to follow the Hebrews betwen the walls of water. As before is here noted out of S. Baſil, and S. Auguſtine [48], and the text itſelf maketh it euident. Againe manie other places confirme, [49] that not God, but the ſinner's owne wilfulnes, is the proper cauſe of his ſinne. Job. 24. v. 23. God hath given him place for penance, and he abuſeth it vnto pride. Eccle. 8. v. 11. Becauſe ſentence is not quickly pronounced againſt the euil, the children of men commit euils without all feare. Oſee. 13. v. 9. Perdition is thine, o Iſrael, only in me thy helpe. Rom. 2. v. 4. The benignitie of God bringeth thee to penance: but according to thy hardneſs, and impenitent heart, thou heapeſt to thyſelf wrath. Ephes. 4. v. 19. Gentiles haue given up themſelues to impudicitie (or vvantonnes.) And manie like places shew, that God is not the mouer, author, nor forcer of anie thing, as it is ſinne: but man himſelf is the author by wilfully conſenting to tentations of the devil, the flesh, and the world, and by abuſing God's benefits, and reſiſting his grace.

annotations.title: They alſo.
annotations.text: [1] [2] True miracles being aboue the courſe of all created nature, can not be wrought but by the power of God; who is truth itſelf, and cannot give teſtimonie to vntruth, and therefore they certainly proue that to be true, for which they are done. [3] [4] Other ſtrange things done by enchanters, falſe prophets, and devils, are not indeed true miracles; but either ſleights, by quicknes and nimblenes of hand, called legier-demain, conueing one thing away and bringing an other; or falſe preſentations deceiuing the ſenſes, and imaginations of men, by making things ſeme to be that they are not; or els are wrought by applying natural cauſes known to ſome, eſpecially to devils; who alſo by their natural force can do great things, when God permitteth them. And ſo by enchantments and certaine ſecrecies, theſe ſorcerers either conueyed away the rods and water, and brought dragons and blood in their place, and more frogs from other places, or els by the devils vſing natural agents turned rods into ſerpents, water into blood, and other matter into frogs: all which might be done naturally in longer time, and by the devil in short time. [5] But manie things are wholy aboue the devils power: as to deſtroy the world: to change the general order thereof: to create of nothing: to raiſe the dead to life: to give ſight to the born blind; and the like, which are only in God's power. In things alſo devils naturally can do, they are much reſtrayned [6] by God's goodnes, leſt they should deceiue or hurt mankind at their pleaſure. So theſe Enchanters fayled in the fourth attempt, not able to make more ſciniphes, nor anie more ſuch prodigies; and were only permitted to produce ſuch ſerpents as were deuoured by Aaron's ſerpent; and to change water into blood; and to increaſe the number of frogs, for the greater plague, and no profit of the Ægyptians. Neither could they remoue anie plague. Nay themſelues were ſo plagued with boyles, that for pain, or for shame, they could not ſtand before Moyſes. [7] It is further to be obſerued, that whenſoeuer anie haue attempted to worke miracles to proue falſe doctrin, they haue failed, and by God's prouidence bene confounded. As when Baals falſe Prophets [8], crying to their falſe gods from morning til noone, could not bring fire for their ſacrifice: and yet the devil brought fire to burne Iobs shepe and ſeruants [9]: God permitting the one, and not the other. [10] God alſo for a time ſuffered Simon Magus to make ſhew of miracles, and at laſt (as Egeſippus li. 3. de excid. Hieroſol. c. 2. and manie others teſtifie) to flie into the air, as though he would haue aſcended into heauen, but S. Peter praying to God, the Magician, notwithſtanding his wings wherewith he preſumed to flie, fell downe and broke his legs, that he could not go. To omitte manie examples, Gregorius Turonenſis li. 2. hiſt. Franc. c. 3. witneſſeth, that one [11] Cyrola an Arian Patriarch, pretending to obtaine of God ſight to a man, that feigned himſelf blind, the man was preſently blind indeed, and exclaiming cryed: Take here thy money which thou gaueſt me to deceiue the world, reſtore me my ſight which I had euen now, and by thy perſuaſion, and for this money, I feigned to want. It happened worſe to one Bruley a poore man in Geneua, whom [12] Caluin with words and money perſuaded to feign himſelf dead, and ſo pretending to raiſe him to life, the man was found dead indeed, and not he but his wife (hauing conſented to the device) lamented in earneſt, inveighing againſt that falſe Apoſtle, calling him a ſecrete thief, and a wicked murderer, that had killed her huſband. So writeth M. Jerome Bolſeck in vita Caluini. And beſides the womans vnexpected out-cry, and aſſeueration that her huſband was not dead before, but that through Caluins perſuaſions and promiſes to relieve them with alms, they ſo feigned, all Geneua did knowe that Caluin endeavoured to raiſe the man, and could not. Theſe and manie others haue attempted and could do nothing, but againſt themſelves. All the danger is when indeed wonders are done that may ſeme to be miracles. Againſt ſuch therefore God's prouidence [13] more particularly aſſiſteth his ſervants diuers ways. [14] Firſt, he warneth all to ſtand faſt when ſuch tentations happen. Deut. 13. If there riſe among you a Prophet, or one that ſaith he hath ſeen a dreame, and foretelleth a ſign, and a wonder, and it cometh to paſſe which he ſpake, and he ſay to thee: Let vs go & folow ſtrange gods, whom thou knoweſt not, and let vs ſerue them, thou ſhalt not heare the words of that Prophet, or dreamer. In like maner our Sauiour foretelling that falſe Chriſts, & falſe-Prophets, ſhal by great ſigns & wonders ſeduce many, warneth all ſaying [15]: Loe I haue foretold you. If therefore they shal ſay vnto you: He is in the deſert, go not out. Behold in the cloſets, believe it not. [16] Secondly, God ſuffered not the Enchanters of Ægypt, nor Simon Magus long: and for the elect, the days of Antichriſt's dangerous perſecution shal be shortened. [17] Thirdly, holy Scripture ſo deſcribeth Antichriſt, as his acts, as when he cometh he may be ſooner knowne. Our Sauiour ſaith: The Jews will receiue him. S. Paul calleth him the man of ſinne [18], importing one ſingular man, and the ſame replete with all wickednes, extolled aboue all that is called God, or is vvorshipped. [19] Neither worshipping true God, nor other falſe god aboue himſelf. [20] He shal be deadly wounded and cured. Not only he shal shew ſtrange wonders, but alſo one of his Prophets shal bring fire from the firmament, & his image ſhal ſpeake. [21] Fourthly, as our Lord gaue power and authoritie to his great Prophet Moyſes againſt the Ægyptian Enchanters, in the end of the law of nature, before the written law, and to his firſt chief Vicar S. Peter, in the beginning of the law of grace, to control & confound Simon Magus: ſo he will ſend his two reſerued great Prophets Enoch and Elias near the end of the world, to reſiſt Antichriſt, and to teach, teſtifie, and confirme with their blood the doctrin of Chriſt. For they ſhal be ſlaine [22], and riſe againe after three days, and aſcend into heauen. Then Antichriſt holding himſelf moſt ſecure, shal ſuddenly be deſtroyed [23]. 2. Theſ. 2. [24]

notes.text: True miracles do certainly proue the truth.
Some strange things done by sleight, by deceipt of senses, & by course of nature, especially by diuels.
Manie things aboue the diuels natural powre.
The diuels powre is much restrained.
False prophets euer faile, when they pretend by miracles to proue their doctrine.
Caluins attempt misproued and he defamed
1 His special warning not to credit preachers of a new Religion, though they pretend to be prophetes, or to worke wonders.
2 Most dangerous seducers reigne but short time.
4 Against most dangerous assaltes God sendeth most forcible resistance.
